scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire study (OpenPROMPT, OpenSAFELY platform, UK NHS data) concerns self-reported and EHR-recorded long COVID and its health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) impact; Lyme disease is never mentioned anywhere in the document.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a UK cohort study (OpenPROMPT, published in The Lancet Regional Health - Europe, 2024) that linked smartphone-collected patient-reported outcome surveys to NHS electronic health records for 6,070 adults to measure how long COVID affects health-related quality of life (HRQoL) using the EQ-5D-5L questionnaire. It found that people who self-reported long COVID had substantially worse quality of life than those who did not, translating into measurable losses of quality-adjusted life-months (QALMs), and that these HRQoL scores were comparable to or worse than those reported elsewhere for heart failure, multiple sclerosis and end-stage renal disease. It also found a large gap between how many people self-reported long COVID (24.6%) and how many had a corresponding diagnosis code in their medical record (under 10%), highlighting a measurement and recognition gap. The study reports no direct medical costs, non-medical costs, or lost-income/productivity figures of its own; it discusses potential workforce and health-service cost implications only qualitatively and by citing other papers.

contextual_issues: The document states that long COVID may cause 'greater economic costs... for a substantial part of the UK workforce, with some individuals reducing their labour output, and others leaving the labour market altogether,' but this claim is supported only by citing an external paper (Reuschke & Houston 2023), not by this study's own data.
The document notes pressure on 'stretched public services' from long COVID care-seeking but does not quantify health-service utilization or direct medical costs itself.
Caregiver time, informal/unpaid care burden, and direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help) are not mentioned or measured anywhere in this document.
Insurance and access barriers are not applicable/discussed in the UK NHS context of this study and are not addressed.

The document notes socioeconomic status (IMD quintile, household income) was associated with HRQoL loss (lower income associated with higher disutility coefficients, Fig. 2) but does not report numeric coefficient values for each income/IMD category in the text.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, non-medical cost, lost-income, or productivity-loss monetary data are reported; translating the QALM/QALY losses into financial costs would require external unit-cost or wage data not supplied by this study.
No data on the date of the COVID-19 episode that led to long COVID relative to symptom onset, preventing modeling of diagnostic delay or time-to-symptom-development.
No HRQoL breakdown by ethnicity was possible; the authors state this directly, attributing it to the low number of non-white respondents in this self-selected cohort.
Follow-up was limited to roughly 3 months (0-90 days); no data exist in this study on QALM/QALY trajectories, costs, or recovery beyond this window without extrapolation.
No caregiver-time or informal-care cost data were collected in this study.
comparison_boundaries: Complete-case QALM totals (0.81 vs. 0.44, N=510, survey completers of all four questionnaires) and available-case QALM totals (0.22 vs. 0.12, N=6513, any completed survey) are structurally different samples with different inclusion criteria and must not be pooled or treated as a simple low/high range of one estimate.

The EHR-diagnosis-stratified QALM analysis (also N=6513, Table 2, 'Long COVID Diagnosis' columns) uses a different case-definition (administrative diagnosis code) than the self-report-based analyses and must not be combined with self-report-based QALM figures as though measuring the same underlying quantity.

Self-reported long COVID (24.6%, survey-based case definition) and EHR-recorded long COVID diagnosis (6%, diagnosis-code-based) are different case definitions capturing different things (patient experience vs. clinical coding) and must not be summed, averaged, or treated as alternate measurements of one 'true' prevalence.

All QALM/QALY and HRQoL figures are specific to this self-selected, UK OpenPROMPT smartphone-app cohort recruited November 2022-July 2023, with HRQoL measured over less than 12 months (0-3 months); none of these figures should be extrapolated to a full year or a lifetime QALY loss without explicitly labeling that as an added assumption beyond the study's own data.

No currency or price-year figures are reported anywhere in this document; any monetary valuation of the QALM/QALY losses described would be a projection requiring external cost-per-QALY or wage-loss data not present in this study.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The study's regression model found an association between gender and reporting a loss of HRQoL (described narratively as one of several demographic predictors alongside comorbidities, shown in Fig. 2, though the specific effect-size for gender is not given as a number in the body text). The study also compared its whole-cohort EQ-5D utility scores to published English population norms that are reported separately by sex (0.798 for females and 0.836 for males, cited from McNamara et al.). Participants who self-identified as non-binary gender were excluded from the EQ-5D utility-mapping analysis because the mapping function only accommodates male/female responses.
sex_gender_findings.source_locator: Results, 'Health-related quality-of-life' (p.7, Fig. 2); Discussion, first paragraph (p.9); Methods, 'EuroQol EQ-5D score' (p.3-4)

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: Table 2's 'Long COVID Diagnosis' columns stratify QALM results by an EHR-recorded long COVID diagnosis code rather than self-report. The document itself states that fewer than 10% of the cohort (6% per Table 1) had such a recorded EHR diagnosis, compared to roughly 25% self-reporting long COVID, indicating this diagnosis-code-based subgroup substantially undercounts the self-reported population.

spec.title: Long COVID Quality-of-Life Burden Simulator (OpenPROMPT UK Cohort)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) and quality-adjusted life-month (QALM) findings from a UK cohort study (OpenPROMPT, N=6,070 adults, surveys linked to NHS records, late 2022-mid 2023, 0-3 month follow-up) comparing people who self-reported long COVID to those who did not. It does NOT contain any direct medical cost, non-medical cost, income-loss, or productivity figures - the source study reports none of its own. It cannot answer insurance, billing, or total-national-cost questions. All quality-of-life figures are specific to this self-selected smartphone-app cohort over a short follow-up window and should not be extrapolated to a full year or a lifetime without labeling that as an added assumption.

takeaway.patient: In this UK study, people who reported long COVID had notably worse day-to-day health status than people who did not, using a standard 0-1 health-status survey (EQ-5D-5L) and a combined measure of health quality over time (quality-adjusted life-months, or QALMs - a score that combines how good your health is with how long you experienced that level). The study also found that many more people reported long COVID on a survey (about 25%) than had a long COVID diagnosis actually recorded in their medical chart (about 6%) - these measure two different things: your own experience versus what got written down in a record, and the study did not determine which one reflects the 'real' number of people affected.
takeaway.care: This cohort found a large, statistically robust association between self-reported long COVID and HRQoL loss (odds ratio 4.7), which shrank markedly (to 1.46, no longer statistically significant) once fatigue and breathlessness patient-reported outcome scores were added to the model - suggesting fatigue and breathlessness account for much of the quality-of-life signal, though breathlessness severity grades themselves were not significant independent predictors of whether a patient reported any loss at all. Separately, only about 6% of this cohort had an EHR-recorded long COVID diagnosis code versus roughly 25% self-reporting it, pointing to a documentation/recognition gap in routine records.
takeaway.policy: This study provides UK cohort-level evidence that self-reported long COVID is associated with substantially reduced HRQoL (odds ratio 4.7, unadjusted) and measurable QALM loss, with quality-of-life scores the authors describe as comparable to or worse than published scores for heart failure, multiple sclerosis, and end-stage renal disease (cited from other sources, not measured here). It also documents a roughly 18.6-percentage-point gap between self-reported long COVID prevalence (24.6%) and EHR-diagnosis-coded prevalence (6%) in this cohort - a measurement/recognition gap, not a validated true-prevalence correction. No cost or productivity data exist in this study to convert these quality-of-life losses into monetary terms.

patient: If you are managing long COVID symptoms, consider discussing with a clinician or patient group how standardized quality-of-life questionnaires (like the EQ-5D-5L) might help put words to day-to-day changes you're experiencing.

If your medical record does not show a long COVID diagnosis even though you experience symptoms, it may help to understand that this UK study found many people in a similar position - this reflects how differently 'self-reported' versus 'chart-recorded' long COVID are counted, not necessarily anything wrong with your own experience.
Consider raising fatigue and breathlessness specifically with your care team, since this study found these two symptoms were strongly linked to reported quality-of-life loss.
care: Consider whether incorporating structured PROMs (EQ-5D-5L, and a fatigue measure such as FACIT-F) into long COVID follow-up visits could help systematically capture the quality-of-life signal this study found, rather than relying on diagnosis coding alone.

This finding may be worth checking against your own documentation workflow: in this cohort, only about 6% of self-reported long COVID cases had a matching EHR diagnosis code, which could understate caseload if used alone for service planning.

Note individually that fatigue was linked to higher odds of reporting any HRQoL loss, while breathlessness severity grades were associated with a larger loss magnitude among those already affected but were not independently significant predictors of whether loss was reported at all - these are two distinct findings and shouldn't be collapsed into one symptom-management message.
policy: Consider whether coding/recognition gaps like the one this cohort documents (25% self-report vs 6% diagnosis-coded) warrant review in surveillance or claims-based case-finding approaches used for long COVID service planning, while keeping in mind this is one self-selected UK cohort, not a national audit.

Use the QALM/EQ-5D findings as an input to severity-of-illness comparisons (e.g., against heart failure, MS, ESRD) for resource-prioritization discussions, labeling clearly that the comparator condition scores come from other, separately cited studies rather than this cohort.

Flag that this pooled estimate has not been disaggregated by race or ethnicity (the authors cite low numbers of non-white respondents as the reason); national survey data sources that support such disaggregation could be considered for a more representative analysis.

Since this study reports no direct cost or productivity-loss data, avoid citing it as a monetary burden estimate; external unit-cost or wage data would be needed to translate these QALM/HRQoL findings into cost terms.

A quality-adjusted life-month combines how good someone's health was with how long they experienced it; a larger positive value here means a bigger measured quality-of-life loss for the long-COVID group over the roughly 3-month follow-up, specific to this complete-case subsample.

outputs.interpretation: Self-reported long COVID (survey case-definition) and EHR-diagnosis-coded long COVID (clinical coding) measure two different things - lived patient experience versus what was formally documented - and the study does not determine which reflects the 'true' number of affected people; which figure is the right one to use depends on the decision being made (e.g., understanding patient experience versus auditing clinical documentation). ## Source
OpenPROMPT study (The Lancet Regional Health - Europe, 2024): a UK cohort of 6,070 adults with smartphone-collected survey responses linked to NHS electronic health records (TPP/OpenSAFELY platform), recruited November 2022-July 2023, with health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) follow-up over roughly 0-3 months.

## What this reproduces
Inputs and outputs are drawn directly from the document's own reported values: mean EQ-5D-5L utility scores (0-1 health-status scale) for self-reported long COVID (0.49) versus non-long COVID (0.71); complete-case total quality-adjusted life-month (QALM) loss figures (0.81 vs 0.44, N=510 survey completers) whose difference reproduces the document's headline 0.37 QALM loss attributable to long COVID; self-reported long COVID prevalence (24.6%) versus EHR-diagnosis-coded prevalence (6%); and odds ratios for reporting any HRQoL loss, unadjusted (4.7) versus adjusted for fatigue/breathlessness PROMs (1.46).

## Limitations
- **Diagnosis-code undercount**: The EHR-diagnosis-coded figure (6%) is based on structured diagnosis codes in primary care records and substantially undercounts the self-reported long COVID population (24.6%) in this cohort; it should not be treated as a complete count of long COVID.
- **No ethnicity breakdown**: The pooled HRQoL/QALM estimates have not been checked for variation by race or ethnicity - the authors state they could not assess this due to low numbers of non-white respondents, even though age, sex, and deprivation quintile were included as model covariates. Federal survey data sources such as NHIS and BRFSS generally support disaggregated analysis by demographic subgroup even though this document did not perform one.
- **Systemic gap**: The document describes a gap between self-reported long COVID (24.6%) and clinical diagnosis coding (under 10%), alongside noting there is no definitive treatment for long COVID, limiting the health system's response beyond symptom tracking and rehabilitation research.
- **Sex/gender**: Gender was included as a regression covariate associated with HRQoL loss, though no numeric effect size is given in the text. Non-binary respondents were excluded from the EQ-5D utility-mapping analysis because the mapping function only accommodates male/female responses. The document separately cites published English population EQ-5D norms of 0.798 (female) and 0.836 (male) for comparison.
- No cost, income, or productivity data appear anywhere in this document; all figures here are quality-of-life/QALM measures only, not monetary.

spec.title: Long COVID Quality-of-Life Burden Simulator (OpenPROMPT UK Cohort)
spec.boundary: This simulation reproduces health-related quality-of-life (HRQoL) and quality-adjusted life-month (QALM) findings from a UK cohort study (OpenPROMPT, N=6,070 adults, surveys linked to NHS records, late 2022-mid 2023, 0-3 month follow-up) comparing people who self-reported long COVID to those who did not. It does NOT contain any direct medical cost, non-medical cost, income-loss, or productivity figures - the source study reports none of its own. It cannot answer insurance, billing, or total-national-cost questions. All quality-of-life figures are specific to this self-selected smartphone-app cohort over a short follow-up window and should not be extrapolated to a full year or a lifetime without labeling that as an added assumption.

takeaway.patient: In this UK study, people who reported long COVID had notably worse day-to-day health status than people who did not, using a standard 0-1 health-status survey (EQ-5D-5L) and a combined measure of health quality over time (quality-adjusted life-months, or QALMs - a score that combines how good your health is with how long you experienced that level). The study also found that many more people reported long COVID on a survey (about 25%) than had a long COVID diagnosis actually recorded in their medical chart (about 6%) - these measure two different things: your own experience versus what got written down in a record, and the study did not determine which one reflects the 'real' number of people affected.
takeaway.care: This cohort found a large, statistically robust association between self-reported long COVID and HRQoL loss (odds ratio 4.7), which shrank markedly (to 1.46, no longer statistically significant) once fatigue and breathlessness patient-reported outcome scores were added to the model - suggesting fatigue and breathlessness account for much of the quality-of-life signal, though breathlessness severity grades themselves were not significant independent predictors of whether a patient reported any loss at all. Separately, only about 6% of this cohort had an EHR-recorded long COVID diagnosis code versus roughly 25% self-reporting it, pointing to a documentation/recognition gap in routine records.
takeaway.policy: This study provides UK cohort-level evidence that self-reported long COVID is associated with substantially reduced HRQoL (odds ratio 4.7, unadjusted) and measurable QALM loss, with quality-of-life scores the authors describe as comparable to or worse than published scores for heart failure, multiple sclerosis, and end-stage renal disease (cited from other sources, not measured here). It also documents a roughly 18.6-percentage-point gap between self-reported long COVID prevalence (24.6%) and EHR-diagnosis-coded prevalence (6%) in this cohort - a measurement/recognition gap, not a validated true-prevalence correction. No cost or productivity data exist in this study to convert these quality-of-life losses into monetary terms.

patient: If you are managing long COVID symptoms, consider discussing with a clinician or patient group how standardized quality-of-life questionnaires (like the EQ-5D-5L) might help put words to day-to-day changes you're experiencing.

If your medical record does not show a long COVID diagnosis even though you experience symptoms, it may help to understand that this UK study found many people in a similar position - this reflects how differently 'self-reported' versus 'chart-recorded' long COVID are counted, not necessarily anything wrong with your own experience.
Consider raising fatigue and breathlessness specifically with your care team, since this study found these two symptoms were strongly linked to reported quality-of-life loss.
care: Consider whether incorporating structured PROMs (EQ-5D-5L, and a fatigue measure such as FACIT-F) into long COVID follow-up visits could help systematically capture the quality-of-life signal this study found, rather than relying on diagnosis coding alone.

This finding may be worth checking against your own documentation workflow: in this cohort, only about 6% of self-reported long COVID cases had a matching EHR diagnosis code, which could understate caseload if used alone for service planning.

Note individually that fatigue was linked to higher odds of reporting any HRQoL loss, while breathlessness severity grades were associated with a larger loss magnitude among those already affected but were not independently significant predictors of whether loss was reported at all - these are two distinct findings and shouldn't be collapsed into one symptom-management message.
policy: Consider whether coding/recognition gaps like the one this cohort documents (25% self-report vs 6% diagnosis-coded) warrant review in surveillance or claims-based case-finding approaches used for long COVID service planning, while keeping in mind this is one self-selected UK cohort, not a national audit.

Use the QALM/EQ-5D findings as an input to severity-of-illness comparisons (e.g., against heart failure, MS, ESRD) for resource-prioritization discussions, labeling clearly that the comparator condition scores come from other, separately cited studies rather than this cohort.

Flag that this pooled estimate has not been disaggregated by race or ethnicity (the authors cite low numbers of non-white respondents as the reason); national survey data sources that support such disaggregation could be considered for a more representative analysis.

Since this study reports no direct cost or productivity-loss data, avoid citing it as a monetary burden estimate; external unit-cost or wage data would be needed to translate these QALM/HRQoL findings into cost terms.

inputs.label: Complete-case QALM loss, self-reported long COVID
inputs.source: Results, 'Individual QALM losses' (p.9); Table 2 (p.12) - complete-case survey completers, N=510
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported cumulative quality-adjusted life-month loss for the self-reported long COVID group among survey completers; raising or lowering it tests how sensitive the attributable-loss output below is to this component value.

inputs.label: Complete-case QALM loss, non-long COVID
inputs.source: Results, 'Individual QALM losses' (p.9); Table 2 (p.12) - complete-case survey completers, N=510
inputs.interpretation: This is the comparator group's reported quality-adjusted life-month loss; it is kept below the long-COVID value's range here because the study's own complete-case result consistently shows the long-COVID group's loss as larger.

inputs.label: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility score, self-reported long COVID
inputs.interpretation: This is the cohort's mean health-status score for people reporting long COVID; moving it shows how the quality-of-life gap below would change if the long-COVID group's average health status were different.

inputs.label: Mean EQ-5D-5L utility score, non-long COVID
inputs.interpretation: This is the comparator group's mean health-status score; its range is kept above the long-COVID group's range because the study consistently reports the non-long-COVID group as healthier on this measure.

inputs.label: Self-reported long COVID (percent of cohort)
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of this UK cohort who reported having long COVID on the survey case-definition questions; comparing it to the diagnosis-code share below illustrates the gap between patient-reported experience and clinical coding in this sample.

inputs.label: EHR-recorded long COVID diagnosis (percent of cohort)
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of the cohort with a formal long COVID diagnosis code in their NHS electronic health record; its range is kept below the self-report range because the study consistently reports fewer coded diagnoses than self-reports in this cohort.

inputs.label: Odds ratio for HRQoL loss, unadjusted
inputs.interpretation: This is the study's reported odds of reporting any HRQoL loss for self-reported long COVID versus not, before adjusting for fatigue/breathlessness scores; comparing it to the adjusted value below shows how much of that association those symptoms may explain.

inputs.label: Odds ratio for HRQoL loss, adjusted for fatigue/breathlessness
inputs.interpretation: This is the odds ratio after adding fatigue and breathlessness patient-reported scores to the model; its range is kept below the unadjusted value's range because the study reports this attenuation consistently, and its confidence interval (0.89-2.38) spans 1, meaning this adjusted association did not reach statistical significance.

outputs.label: Complete-case QALM loss difference, long COVID minus non-long COVID (positive = long COVID group had greater measured quality-adjusted life-month loss)
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the study's reported 0.37 QALM loss attributable to self-reported long COVID using its own separately reported complete-case component values (N=510, survey completers). A quality-adjusted life-month combines how good someone's health was with how long they experienced it; a larger positive value here means a bigger measured quality-of-life loss for the long-COVID group over the roughly 3-month follow-up, specific to this complete-case subsample.

outputs.label: EQ-5D-5L utility score, long COVID minus non-long COVID (negative = lower quality of life among those reporting long COVID)
outputs.interpretation: This is the difference between the two groups' mean health-status scores on a 0-1 scale where 1 is full health. The study reports this gap as negative (long-COVID group scoring lower); a more negative value here would mean a larger measured quality-of-life gap between the two groups in this cohort.

outputs.label: Self-reported long COVID percent minus EHR-diagnosis-coded percent (positive = more people self-reported long COVID than had a diagnosis code on record)
outputs.interpretation: Self-reported long COVID (survey case-definition) and EHR-diagnosis-coded long COVID (clinical coding) measure two different things - lived patient experience versus what was formally documented - and the study does not determine which reflects the 'true' number of affected people; which figure is the right one to use depends on the decision being made (e.g., understanding patient experience versus auditing clinical documentation). A larger positive value here means a wider gap between the two measures in this cohort.

outputs.label: Unadjusted minus PROMs-adjusted odds ratio for HRQoL loss (positive = odds ratio shrank after adjusting for fatigue and breathlessness scores)
outputs.unit: odds ratio points (difference in odds ratios)
outputs.interpretation: This shows how much the association between self-reported long COVID and reporting HRQoL loss weakens once fatigue and breathlessness scores are included in the model. The study's unadjusted odds ratio (statistically significant) dropped to an adjusted value whose confidence interval spanned 1 (no longer statistically significant per the document); a larger positive value here means fatigue/breathlessness account for more of the original association in this cohort's model.
